utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having concluded the hearing on the motion under Article 98 bis, we will now continue with a Status Conference. Before starting with the Status Conference, I would like to stress that it may be clear to the parties that only today the Chamber heard the oral arguments on the motion, that we still have to deliberate on the decision to be taken, and that therefore, what we are discussing now is just for preparing for the situation, and not one of us knows at this moment whether this situation ever will exist, that the motion will be wholly or partially denied. So we are preparing in case of that the Defence will have to present its case. I wanted to make this quite clear, and it is mainly practical matters that we are dealing with. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence is conscious and aware of that and we thank you for it. Just simply that I would like to ask you for your leave to leave as of 14.13. I have already told Madam Registrar I have a plane to catch. And with your leave, I would leave, and of course my colleagues will remain here and the Defence will be perfectly well represented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to work as efficiently as possible, but you are excused if you have to catch a plane. I would first like to have a list of some items the Chamber would like to raise and then, of course, there would be an opportunity for the parties to raise any additional necessary at that moment. I first would like to go back to what happened before the summer recess. We have 92 bis statements, some of them tendered. They were all filed under the P Exhibit Number 3663 and then later some letters were added. The Chamber would like the Prosecution especially to retender the partially admitted statements, and then redact it in such a way that taken out the parts not admitted, so that the admitted parts of the statements are remaining and they would be retendered. And then giving the following exhibit numbering, that would be, Madam Registrar, P3663C, I think we start. This especially in respect of the Witness Soubirou and Rakic partially admitted. There is another remaining issue. Exhibits PT289 is a booklet of which the Prosecution asked the Registry to return the original to the witness. It has been dealt with. We have given a decision that a copy would be made of that booklet and that the original would be returned to the witness. As far as I understand, the original seems to not be the in the hand of the Registry at this moment. I don't know whether this needs any specific attention at this moment. No, if you say that it doesn't need any specific attention, then I take it that the problem have been solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, but we are looking elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, I would like to turn into private session for the next issue we have to deal with that relates to the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session now again. In your filing of the 19th of September, it appears that all the documents have been disclosed to the Prosecution, so that you have fulfilled -- that the Defence fulfilled its obligation fully at this very moment. Of course, apart from the ongoing obligations, since there is reciprocal disclosure to continue. But as it stands now, everything has been disclosed to the Prosecution. The Prosecution does not agree. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence and the Prosecution met yesterday afternoon. We informed the Defence that we have not received the 16 newspaper articles. We have not received two of the six books. And we also have not received a reasonably large number of documents which appear in the exhibit list. We have given the Defence a list of those documents, and we are told by the Defence that by this coming Monday, the 23rd of September, we will have a list of the newspaper articles. And in due course, we will have disclosed to us the two additional books, and we will receive a response in relation to the number of other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution and the Defence had a meeting yesterday. We were speaking of newspaper articles. The Defence is of the position that they have already disclosed them to the Prosecution. However, I don't have the documentation confirming when this was disclosed, and this is why I told the Prosecution that I will verify which documents have been disclosed so far. I believe that these newspaper articles have been disclosed, together with the two missing books that have not been found by the Prosecution yet. Now, as far as the list of the documents is concerned, the Prosecution gave us a list of the documents that they believe are missing. And I promised my colleagues I would verify this and inform them on Monday exactly when the newspaper articles and two books were disclosed, as well as the list of documents that the Prosecution claims they are missing. So, on Monday I will contact my colleagues with further information regarding this. Another matter that we touched upon is the translation of exhibits. The Defence has translated some of the exhibits. If we are going to touch upon these later, then I will refrain from speaking on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have exhibits as the next issue on my list. I would first try to finish with disclosure, as such. So I take it that there is a constructive cooperation between the parties, and that the still remaining could be solved in relatively short time. Then we come to the exhibit list. First of all, I noticed that - and I think it was done on the request of the Registry - all the exhibits -- I should say, as a matter of fact, documents, because they become exhibits once they are tendered and admitted, but all the documents have been prenumbered, at least we see on the list that they have all got numbers. So from now on, the list of exhibits admitted will not be in the subsequent order, but according to the prenumbering that has been made on the list at this very moment. I understood that as far as the exhibits are concerned, there were no objections by the Prosecution at this moment on the authenticity of the documents. At the same time I noticed this morning that you, Mr. Ierace, made an observation as far as authenticity not even be checked. What is the position of the Prosecution on authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on a number of occasions over the last six months, I have made requests of the Defence, both Mr. Piletta-Zanin and Madam Pilipovic, in order to ascertain the authenticity of the SRK documents which have been disclosed by them to us, such as, I have requested the opportunity - which I am entitled to under Rule 66 - to see and examine the originals. I have also requested information as to where the documents were found. On each of the numerous occasions I have made that request, I have been told that they would get back to me and that never happened. I was, therefore, surprised to see that there was no issue as to authenticity. At the meeting yesterday, I made it clear that the position of the Prosecution is that we cannot acknowledge the authenticity of the documents unless we have such information made available to us and an opportunity to make our own enquiries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the authenticity issue is not settled yet. Ms. Pilipovic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what my colleague just said, that we discussed the authenticity of documents yesterday. In relation to this, I would like to tell you that I contacted my investigators regarding this. From the very beginning of this trial, I have informed the Trial Chamber that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was disbanded after the Dayton Agreement. And I also told you that the documentation of the corps could be found all over the territory of Republika Srpska. All of the documents that the Defence has disclosed during the past 18 months to the Prosecution were initially obtained by our investigators, and the originals of these documents can be found in Banja Luka in the main depository. My investigators have told me that the documents they found in the field were found in Nevesinje Pale, Rogatica Pale, and there is other places. Therefore, the documents that are in possession of the Defence and that had been disclosed to us -- by us to the Prosecution, the originals of these documents are with the military authorities in Banja Luka. Therefore, my colleagues can gain access to all of these documents in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you are telling us is that you have no originals available. You are under an obligation -- I think it is not under Rule 66, but under Rule 67(C) where it says if the Defence has made a request under 66(B), The Prosecution should be entitled to respect any books, et cetera. That is Rule 67(C), That you may inspect the copies in the hands of the Defence, but I also do understand that copies have been made and have been made available to you. And for the originals, that you should apply for access in Banja Luka. But at least you indicated where the documents you copied for your own file are kept at this -- where these documents are kept, and you say in Banja Luka in the general storage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the copies of the documents that were disclosed by the Defence were obtained from our investigators. And I told you that the originals of these documents can be found in Banja Luka in the Main Staff there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we sufficiently then discussed the issue of authenticity. Of course, it is of no use to go through the authenticity of all the documents at this very moment. We will see what happens when some or all of these documents will be tendered into evidence and then see whether there is any authenticity objection remaining. Then the next issue translation. Ms. Pilipovic, do I understand you well that all the documents you intend to tender into evidence are translated by now?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the majority of the documents have been translated. The Defence is still trying to ensure that the documents that will be tendered during the Defence case are translated. Yesterday, I agreed in the discussion with my colleagues. I heard from them that they are able to provide assistance in translating these documents. Therefore, we agreed that some of the documents that the Defence intends to introduce during the first weeks of our case, will be delivered to our colleagues so that they can assist us in translating these documents. I believe that this is what we agreed on yesterday, if I properly understood my colleagues. At any rate, we will do our best to have the documents translated, those that we intend to tender during our case, and delivered to our colleagues within the prescribed time of seven days before we intend to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us any idea at this moment, 80 per cent or 60 per cent or 95 per cent of the documents that you intend to tender are translated? Just an approximate idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think that we have 50 per cent translated yet. However, the Defence believes that we will be able to comply with the ruling of this Trial Chamber, and to forward the documents seven days prior to tendering them. We have been assured by the Prosecution that they will try to assist us in having these documents translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it is the rule not later than seven days; that is a different thing than seven days before. The earlier, the better. So if there are any documents at this moment that you know already that you will tender, provide them already for translation so that the parties have an opportunity to -- that the Prosecution has an opportunity to study them already. And also keep in mind that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is what we arranged, Your Honour, with the other side. I think that as early as Monday we will be able to indicate which documents on the list that we discussed will be used during the first few weeks of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may have notice in the Scheduling Order Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the Chamber is specifically concerned about timely translation. So let's -- unless the Prosecution has any further submissions to make in this respect, let's just for a moment forget about the detailed written reports on the efforts you have made, because I -- as the Chamber sees, a lot of progress has already been made. But if there is any additional submission to be made, Mr. Ierace, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. I want to be crystal clear on this issue of translations so that the Defence problem doesn't become the Prosecution problem. As I understand it, 130 of the Defence documents have been translated. And we were given copies of those yesterday, and they are the first 130 documents on the list which was filed yesterday. I offered to assist the Defence on this basis: That we could perhaps have a language assistant prepare a rough translation of the documents, not a draft translation and not a formal translation, and we would be more than happy to make those translations available to the Defence and the Trial Chamber. We could not do them all in a short space of time, and therefore, if they -- if the Defence, if it did not imperil their case, were prepared to tell us which documents they will be tendering in the first three weeks, perhaps one week straight away, two weeks very quickly, then we would prioritize those documents and as soon as we get them, we will make them available. And, of course, that assumes that a rough translation will be acceptable to the -- to Your Honours. So we will do that. Mr. President, there is however another issue, and that is the books and the tapes. I have asked the Defence to indicate which paragraphs of the books they wish to tender so that we don't have to embark on translating six books. And they are quite thick. And secondly, we have received now I think 23 videotapes. So I think well in excess of 100 hours of viewing. I could be wrong on that, but I think it is in excess of 100. I don't know what steps have been taken by the Defence to provide a transcript of those videotapes and a translation into English. And I hesitate to offer the services of the Prosecution to do that for them. I am not sure that we have those resources. But perhaps that could be dealt with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please respond to that, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when it comes to video material, those segments that the Defence intends to tender will be taken care of by us, meaning that we will provide the transcripts for the segments that we intend to tender. We have already started working on this, and I have transcripts prepared already for some portion of the video material. I will do my best to do this on a timely -- in a timely manner for all other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would be grateful if we knew when we could expect to have the parts of the books identified, that will be tendered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic. Having gone through the videos, you now have to also read books, as far as I understand. Did you identify already the parts of the books, and could you inform the Prosecution about it , because otherwise, they have to read books as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is doing its utmost in that respect, as well. We will try to inform the Prosecution as soon as possible about the parts that we intend to use. And this is something I informed my colleagues yesterday. I also told them that if we had two more assistants, I am sure that we would be able to be more efficient in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that is a matter of the Registry, rather than a matter of the Prosecution. I get the feeling that there is some constructive cooperation in this field as well, or fields, as repeating the words of Judge Rodrigues, who used these terms quite regularly. So I take it that the video will have priority, and you have already identified and you will take care of that so that you could inform the Prosecution about that. And the books are coming next. May I ask the Prosecution to remind the Chamber if they feel that the Defence is losing pace in making progress in respect of the videos and the books? Because we have no firm answer at this very moment, but of course it is of no use perhaps to say at this moment, it should be done in ten days. Let's just see how we proceed, and if the Prosecution would remind the Chamber that they think it would need more attention than it gets at that very moment. Then that's about the exhibits. Then I would like to turn to the witness list which has been filed yesterday as far as I see. The Scheduling Order asked the Defence to list the witness in different categories - such as those used by the Defence in the provisional list - within each category by order of importance for the Defence case. I see that the list, as it is now, does not categorise the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witnesses in the same way as the provisional list did. And I don't know whether this is the order of priority or that it still has to be done, Ms. Pilipovic. Because it is -- gives me the impression that it is not specifically in an order of priority for the Defence case, but I might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has done its best to categorise the witnesses. They are all important to the Defence. And we made the concerted effort to go through the witnesses according to list and represent them as they will appear. One of the most efficient ways for the Defence was that the witnesses would obviously come to the court and testify. One of the main problems that the Defence had was the changes of passport, because this started in Republika Srpska on the 21st of July of this year. So all of the witnesses had to have their passports changed, although the witnesses already had their passports. So the Defence think it is best to do all these witnesses, 76 of them, to put them in some kind of order of importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. By category then, because you changed the categories. It was not without reason that in the Scheduling Order that the Chamber referred to the categories. Because the Chamber was of the opinion was quite helpful to have them in these categories, and then of course within these categories to be listed in priority order. But these categories we now have to reconstruct them. Of course, for some of the witnesses, it is possible to see whether they are UNMOs or not, but not for all of them. So if the original categorization could be restored and then have them listed in whether it is -- whether they are more important or not than other witnesses. As you know, it is like equals. Some people are more equal than others. And I do understand that all of the witnesses are important for the Defence, but some might be of greater importance than others.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will have a second look to the list of the witnesses, and we hope that we will do this as soon as possible to somehow categorise them according to some order the way the Trial Chamber wishes it. I apologise, Your Honour. We are not going to be able to be able to ascertain that the witness will follow this order absolutely as they are submitted. They will be brought to the Tribunal. I think that is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I ask you to categorise, that is for other reasons than the appearances of the witnesses in court. That is, of course, a totally different whether you want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we asked for a list of not more than 170 hours. There is one witness of which is not certain whether he will testify or not. But if he would testify, we would have a total of 186 hours. That is more than 170. So I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We checked this yesterday, last night, after we looked at the list again. And this has also been spotted by the Defence as a problem, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you would -- so that's the list in that respect does not yet meet the requirements put by the Chamber. Are there any comments to be made at this moment on the list of the witnesses, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I note that it is a significantly different list from the one filed earlier. I have only seen it for the first time this morning. I also note that two things, that at least one of the witnesses, an international, as I understand it, was not in Sarajevo in the indictment period, perhaps a few days after he left. That is an issue of preliminary relevance. Secondly, a number of the witnesses, according to the descriptions, appear to be giving evidence which is irrelevant to the issues before the Trial Chamber, either entirely, according to the descriptions, or at least in the majority. And by that I mean descriptions to the effect that they will give evidence about targeting of civilians on the side of the confrontation line held by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Two or three times so far, the issue of tu quoque. Tu quoque has appeared to arise and we have been assured by the Defence, that it would not be put forward as a Defence. It is quite predictable that much time will be taken up with these witnesses, based on these descriptions, arguing over just that issue. Mr. President, in those circumstances, might I respectfully submit that there should be some initial deliberation on this issue in the interests of predictably saving argument with a great many of these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witnesses. In other words, it should be made perfectly clear what is and is not admissible in terms of subject matter. And by that I mean, if the Defence wishes to submit that it is relevant, then perhaps that can be more economically done rather than in the context of individual witnesses. At the outset in terms of general parameters, it may mean that a large number of these witnesses either don't have relevant evidence or at least their relevant evidence is very short. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the Chamber received -- some members of the Chamber received this list yesterday. Some of them have seen it only this morning. So I think we cannot discuss this matter at this very moment, where it was even suggested to the Chamber to do so, we decided that we will deal with it at the pre-Defence conference. But it would be helpful if the parties would prepare written submissions so that we can first read what the objections are and then perhaps specify for specific witnesses, and then receive a response from the Defence, so that we can more efficiently deal with it at the pre-Defence conference. So may I invite you first, Mr. Ierace, to file submissions in that respect from the Prosecution's view. I would say that, giving this order today, that if you wish that you have to file written submissions, that the same time you need to prepare them, they will be given to the Defence to respond. Yes? The witness list, we -- the Chamber has seen that -- are there any other submissions to be made in respect of the witness list, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber observed that quite many witnesses are seeking, or at least the Defence is seeking for quite many witnesses, protective measures. I would say it is rather become a rule than the exception. We have not seen any requests, but the Scheduling Order says that by the 25th of September, the requests should be submitted to the Chamber. And since we see that it is known already for many witnesses that the reasons are given, so that we can listen to the argument and to the response of the Prosecution. I must say it is a quite high number. And as we sometimes disencouraged the Prosecution to stick to the protective measures sought, and seeking protective measures for far less -- for a number far less of witnesses, the Defence is certainly aware that this Chamber is very much -- is paying a lot of attention to the public character of the trial, and, therefore, would like to ask the Defence also to keep in mind the important aspect of the publicity of this trial. We will see whether this would reduce the number of applications for protective measures. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave, the Defence has heard all your remarks and observations and will do its utmost to take them into consideration. However, this situation is different from the Prosecution's, and here I hesitate to tell you about my personal experience, but I will perhaps do it one day, people who come and -- who come from the side of vanquished, they are still today much more prone to defuse emotions rather than those who come from the triumphant side. Now, this is what explains it. These people are in a different position and this is what we have to say, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the Defence takes it that -- this is partly argument already. Let's just weight and see what the reasons are given for the request for protective measures, and then we will then decide after having heard the response of the Prosecution. If you are about to leave, I just tell you what was still on the agenda. So it was the videolink, when we can expect an application for the videolink, because that is what the Defence asks. And another thing the Chamber would like to raise is points of agreements between the parties which is an unsettled issue still already since the 16th of November last year. And finally, I would deal, so that you would know and if you want to deal -- when you want to discuss it with Ms. Pilipovic just for one minute, that it would be possible, I would like to pay attention to the fact that the Chamber was not quite amused by both parties using more pages or longer pages than they should have done in accordance with the guidelines. And finally, I would like to pay attention to the health situation of the accused. So that was on my agenda, so that you know what you are missing, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. With your leave, I shall depart. And thank you again for myself and in the name of the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, so the first issue was when do you intend to file a motion for videolink? When could we expect it, approximately? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as the situation stands now, the Defence believes that that will be after the 25th of October. So between the 25th of October and 6th of November. We have two witnesses in the Sarajevo area who expressed the wish to testify via videolink. Now, we have a problem with a couple more witnesses who, for medical reasons, would not be able to come to the Tribunal. So we will try that by the 25th of October and by 6th of November, that between these two dates, the Defence witnesses will testify by videolink, all focused in one location to make it easier. But I will have to say that perhaps there will be some witnesses who will want to testify by videolink and that it should be done from Belgrade. The Defence has one witness who lives in Novi Sad, and whose medical condition is currently such a state that he cannot guarantee that he will be able to come to The Hague. And we have one witness who is unfortunately -- who has unfortunately now become very ill, and he thinks that he will not be able to travel. But this will depend on his tests. But the Defence will make sure that the Defence knows by the time and that we will be able to inform by the time and the location. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's about the videolink. I do understand that it is mainly for medical reasons that you are seeking witnesses to testify by videolink. There are also a number of witnesses under 92 bis. When do you expect to have their statements to be available to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence assesses that this will happen in the next month, that it will be in a month's time that we will be able to have this checked, that an officer of the Registry will be able to confirm these statements. This should happen as soon as possible, of course, but generally, I think it will be in a month's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking this because the officer has to be appointed, has to travel to the locality where the witness resides. So I would like to -- we will consider whether somewhere in the next month would be good enough that we would urge you to even do it quicker. But we will -- we will give it specific attention. Next question is about expert witnesses. When do you expect that you could submit the reports of the expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has also discussed this question. And in our assessment, it will be early November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Early November. Of course it very much depends on what will be the order of calling your witnesses and expert witnesses, whether this would be in due time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will check again what exactly our ruling was for the Prosecution, because I remember that we had a very specific ruling on how much time the other party would need to express itself, whether it would accept the expert report, and how much time there would still be needed to prepare for the appearance of that expert witness in court. But at least it is in the transcript now, that it's your expectation it will be the beginning of November. Mr. Ierace, would there be any specific responses or submissions to be made on the issues we just dealt with, that is, protective measures, videolink, 92 bis, and expert reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Mr. President. I was unsure from what my learned colleague said as to the dates for the videolink testimony. Was she suggesting that the testimony would occur between the 25th of October and the 6th of November? Because if that is the case, I wonder whether we have enough time to decide if it is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand that you would file the motion between these two dates. Is that correct? Or would you like to have the videolink effective in these -- this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, at that period of time, Your Honour. But unfortunately, I received this information only now, when I was in Sarajevo. So I was not able to do anything about it earlier. One important witness for the Defence, just like all the others, this witness asked for the testimony to happen between the 25th of October and 6th of November, and that is why I was speaking to other witnesses who will also testify via videolink. That is how I specified this time and this is what I have just told the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I apologise, but I would just like to know, what is the delay that is needed so that we would be as efficient as possible to inform the parties for the videolink? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have two issues. First whether the Chamber allows the witness to be examined by videolink; and then the second is the technical preparation for it. So the first thing that has to be done anyhow is to apply for it rather soon. Then the Chamber will try to find the answer to the next question: How much time it would need to prepare for the videolink to be established. Because it is not just the technicalities, but also someone of the Registry being present. So therefore, if you apply as soon as possible for the permission to have these witnesses heard by videolink, examined by videolink, we will then at the same time try to find out how much time it would take to prepare. The next issue is: Points of agreement between the parties. I noticed that in the pre-trial -- some of the pre-trial Status Conferences, that the parties seem to agree on certain issues. I am specifically referring to the 16th of November of last year. And there was still a long list where the parties were supposed to sign this list as being the points on which the parties would agree. Finally, for this agreement on few points, the list as such was not signed and was not filed. Although you might wonder whether or not some of these facts were facts of common knowledge. I don't know whether the parties really still disagree on Sarajevo being on the east/west axis in the valley. I don't think so, as a matter of fact. And a lot of other issues I think the parties could easily agree upon. And perhaps the list could be a bit longer. For example, I wonder, having read the motion under Rule 98 bis whether the -- for example, the Defence contests that witnesses of certain incidents, that some people were injured during these incidents. For example, Witness A, B, C, or D, that is Witness A was injured at a spot, at a certain date. I am not talking about the hour of the day, because that sometimes is in dispute. But whether -- I never heard we put to the witness that you just claimed to have been hit by a bullet, but you were not. So a lot of issues, I think, could be easily dealt with. And I also thought of confrontation lines because we have evidence from some witnesses on confrontation lines. Then as an attachment to the motion under Rule 98 bis, we are confronted with a map which also indicates confrontation lines. And I am not saying that they are for every centimetre the same, but they very much look alike I must say. So therefore, and that does not even differentiate to times of the conflict. But especially since I also read that a lot of the witnesses of the Defence would testify on the establishment and on the situation of confrontation lines, I wondered, how much disagreement is there on the actual position of the confrontation lines and whether we could limit ourselves to -- well, to those parts in dispute, of those parts of the confrontation lines very relevant for a specific incident or those parts of the confrontation lines moving during the conflict considerably rather than hear another 10, 20, or 30 witnesses on where approximately the confrontation lines were. So these are just two suggestions on which the Chamber would like to invite the parties to sit together again and to see what could be reached. And if you would need any assistance to that, the Chamber is quite willing to assist you in it or the Senior Legal Officer could perhaps assist. So there might be ways to finish what remained unaccomplished last year on the 16th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I respond to that very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would, for my part, for the Prosecution part, be grateful for that assistance. We did meet to go through the propositions that were provided to us by Judge Rodrigues. And it may be that at this stage, more could be accomplished by us. I think that the presence of an assisting party, either the Court or the Court through the Senior Legal Officer, may be a positive contribution towards achieving that result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I may just spend a few words on that again. I remember that -- I have not been present but -- the mere fact of whether an appointment started on the 10th of October, or the 8th or the 9th or the 7th or the 6th was one of the points of disagreement at that moment. As far as the Chamber is aware, this has not been a hot issue during the last seven months, but it was the 6th, the 7th, the 8th, the 9th, or the 10th. So therefore, even if you compromise, even could say that the parties agree that on or around the 8th of September, so that if someone wants to establish that it is within this time limit. Because it is a pity that you have to spend a lot of the time on these kind of issues if they are such small differences. And perhaps you can also then see how important these differences turn out to be. So if the parties could sit together and see whether they could achieve more than they did last year, that would be highly welcomed by the Chamber. Then, the final point I would like to raise is the page limit for filings. The Chamber noticed that both parties have sought different ways of achieving the same, that is, to use more pages than allowed. The Defence did it by putting 400 words on a page instead of 300, which is in accordance with the guidelines, and the Prosecution did it by asking for more pages at the very moment when the document was filed. I don't think it needs any words to say that the Chamber is not amused by the different techniques used to do what the parties apparently want to do, but should not do. Then, the final and a more important issue, and that would be the last one for the Chamber to raise, but of course the parties will have an opportunity to raise any additional issue. General Galic, the Chamber would like to know whether there are any developments in your health situation that would need the attention of the Chamber at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sorry. There are no important changes. I can just tell you that in the last month --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. As you know, as before, if you would rather speak about it in private session, the Chamber is - for reasons of your privacy - perfectly willing to go into private session. I leave it up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for warning me, but I don't think there is anything secret about this. I think that we can speak normally, because the question that we have spoken about is already known. In the last month, I have used -- since the detention administration helped me, I went to have physiotherapy on several occasions. There has been some progress -- at least that is what I feel. But there have been also some crisis, and even on one occasion, I had even asked to have surgery. I hope that for the rest of the trial, together with the doctors, I will do my best to follow the trial, to be at the trial, and to follow the trial under normal circumstances. But if there are any considerable problems, I will inform you in due course. For the time being, I feel that I am able to follow the trial. Now I have my family who is visiting me today, and I hope that this will also contribute to an improved mood. And you know everything happens in the mind and everything begins and ends with the brain. So I hope that once the trial begins, I will be refreshed for the continuation of the trial. Thank you very much, and thank you for your concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, General Galic, for informing us. It is good to hear that you aware that if there is anything to be brought to the attention of the Chamber, that you can do so, and the Chamber expects you to do so. Apart from that, I am glad to hear that at least the physiotherapy gives some relief, although not the final solution, of course. And then now I am urging the parties to proceed quickly, because your family is waiting. Is there any other issue the parties would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand that we are sitting again -- is it the 2nd of October?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The pre-Defence conference is scheduled for the -- I think it was for the -- I should have a look at my --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar is nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's better to rely upon her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The Defence and I are meeting the day before, and I am sure that we will both do what we can to finalise the more obvious issues of fact. And perhaps once we have done that, we can indicate what issues may perhaps, if we both agree, benefit by some outside assistance. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever you need the assistance of the Chamber or the Senior Legal Officer, you know how to apply for it. Anything to be raised by the Defence, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I just wanted to check whether it is on the 3rd or on the 2nd? I think that the Status Conference is on the 3rd and that our meeting with the Prosecution is on the 2nd, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I see, the pre-Defence conference will be on October 3rd at 9.00 in the morning. Yes. Yes, I am asked to remind you that, of course, you should inform the Victims and Witness Unit in due time for the first witnesses for which you need the assistance of transferring them to The Hague, so that you are well prepared for the 7th of October. Yes -- of course, not the 7th of October, perhaps not the first witness but at least they need time to prepare it, and that you get in touch with them in due time. Yes. Okay, then this concludes the Status Conference. I Thank the parties for the cooperation, and we will see each other again at the 3rd of October.
